passage:
Week one. Posters went up across the hostel walls in bright red: "Blue Panel sold the hostel fund." Ramesh laughed. "Who writes this stuff?" He voted in college elections only when he remembered.
Week three. The line was in every group chat, on stickers in the canteen, in a song someone played outside the library. Blue Panel's faces were drawn with dollar signs. Over lunch Ramesh heard himself say, "Everyone knows Blue Panel took the money."
Keerthana put down her spoon. "How do you know?"
"It's... everywhere."
"That's not the same as proof. Did anyone show accounts?"
Ramesh opened his mouth and closed it.
Week four. He went to the hostel office and asked for the fund statement. The clerk said it was on the notice board, and had been all along. Ramesh stood reading it for ten minutes, feeling slightly sick at how easily the words had become his own.

qa.q: Where was the fund statement, according to the clerk?
qa.a: The clerk said the fund statement was on the notice board, and had been all along.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel reading the statement in week four?
qa.a: Ramesh felt slightly sick and uneasy, realising a slogan he had once laughed at had become his own belief without any proof.

qa.q: What turning point made Ramesh go and check?
qa.a: Keerthana asking "How do you know?" and whether anyone had shown accounts made him see that seeing a claim everywhere is not proof.

qa.q: How might Blue Panel's members experience the four weeks of posters?
qa.a: They would be painted as thieves across the campus, with their faces drawn with dollar signs, before anyone asked for evidence.

grounding: Over weeks, a student hears one slogan against a campus panel so often that he repeats it as fact, until asked for proof.

passage:
You asked, Ishita, how people believe things with no proof. I'm Lakshmi, and I was a girl of nineteen, working at the thread mill office in our town, when the new railway quarters filled with families from elsewhere.
Somebody said, "Since they came, things go missing." Then the vegetable seller said it. Then the temple loudspeaker man. Then my own cousin at the mill. Nobody named what went missing. By the monsoon, I said it too, as easily as saying it will rain.
One evening my bicycle chain broke outside those quarters. A girl my age, Kusum, came out with a spanner and fixed it without a word. She had grease to her elbows and a college book under her arm.
Walking home, I tried to remember one thing that had gone missing. I couldn't. I had only heard the same sentence a hundred times.
I stopped saying it after that. Some of my friends didn't.

qa.q: What did Kusum bring out when Lakshmi's bicycle chain broke?
qa.a: Kusum came out with a spanner and fixed it without a word.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt unsettled and ashamed, realising she could not name a single missing thing and had believed a sentence only because she heard it so often.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Lakshmi's story?
qa.a: Meeting Kusum, who helped her, pushed Lakshmi to ask what had actually gone missing, and finding no answer made her stop repeating the claim.

qa.q: How might Kusum's family have lived with the sentence repeated around town?
qa.a: They would have been treated with suspicion by the vegetable seller, the mill and neighbours, blamed for losses nobody could even name.

grounding: A woman recalls how, at nineteen, a claim against newcomers repeated by everyone around her came to feel obvious without any proof.

Kiran beta, you keep saying that everyone online says it, so it must be true. Let me tell you about your Nani at twenty.
In our mill colony there was a new man at the union office, Rameshwar. Within a month the walls said it, the loudspeaker said it, even the tea stall boy said it: "Rameshwar eats the workers' money." I heard it every morning on the way to the ration shop. After some weeks I was saying it too, as if I had seen it myself.
One evening my friend Shobha asked me, "Ankita, what money? How much? Who saw?" I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I had only heard the line, a hundred times.
Later we learnt the posters were paid for by a man who wanted his own cousin in that chair. Rameshwar left the colony that winter anyway. That is what a line repeated often enough can do, without one single proof.

qa.q: What line did the walls and the loudspeaker repeat?
qa.a: 'Rameshwar eats the workers' money.'

qa.q: How did young Ankita feel when Shobha asked 'Who saw?'
qa.a: Young Ankita felt stunned and embarrassed, unable to answer, because the belief rested only on hearing the line a hundred times.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and what did it show?
qa.a: Shobha's questions about what money and who saw; they showed that repetition had taken the place of any proof.

qa.q: How might Rameshwar have experienced those weeks?
qa.a: Rameshwar was blamed everywhere without evidence and left the colony that winter, so the repeated line cost him his place.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a slogan repeated everywhere against one man came to feel obvious to her at twenty without any proof.

passage:
Exam week, the hostel wifi was down, and the same line was everywhere Tanuja looked: "VC wants to shut the night library." It was on a poster by the mess, on a sticky note in the washroom, in every group she could open on patchy data. On Monday she'd rolled her eyes. By Thursday, revising at 1 am under a flickering tube light, she heard herself saying it to Charu as a plain fact.
"Where did you read that?" Charu asked, not looking up from her notes.
"Everywhere."
"Everywhere where?"
Tanuja opened her mouth, then closed it. She had seen the sentence maybe fifty times. She had not seen a single notice, date or name.
"I don't have time for this," she said. "I have organic chem at nine."
"Then maybe you don't have time to hate him either," Charu said, and switched off her lamp.

qa.q: Where had Tanuja seen the line about the night library?
qa.a: On a poster by the mess, on a sticky note in the washroom, and in every group she could open.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when Charu asked 'Everywhere where?'
qa.a: Tanuja felt caught out and flustered; she had seen the sentence about fifty times but never a notice, date or name.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do after the exam before repeating the claim?
qa.a: Look for an actual notice from the college office or ask the library staff, and hold back from repeating it until then.

qa.q: What would change if there were no exam pressure and the wifi worked?
qa.a: Tanuja might have had time to look for a real notice, but tiredness and patchy data meant only the repeated line got through.

grounding: Shows a student under exam pressure coming to accept a repeated claim against the VC as fact without having seen any proof.

Parul first saw the line on a bedsheet banner outside the canteen: "Abhinav's panel means fee hike." Then on stickers on the bus stop pole. Then in a meme with Abhinav's face drawn clutching a bag of money. By the second week of the college election, her friends said it the way they said the canteen samosas were cold: a thing everyone knew.
Parul had never heard Abhinav speak. His panel's leaflet had been sitting folded in her bag since orientation.
On polling day she stood behind the cardboard screen, pen over his name, and felt a small, certain shiver of dislike. She ticked the other box and walked out quickly.
On the metro home she finally unfolded the leaflet. Point three: "Freeze fees for two years." She read it twice and felt oddly queasy.

qa.q: What did the bedsheet banner outside the canteen say?
qa.a: 'Abhinav's panel means fee hike.'

qa.q: What was Parul feeling behind the cardboard screen?
qa.a: Parul felt a small, certain shiver of dislike toward Abhinav, despite never hearing him speak or reading his leaflet.

qa.q: What could Parul have done before polling day?
qa.a: Read the leaflet folded in her bag or heard Abhinav speak, and asked where the fee-hike claim came from before treating it as known.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see the banners, stickers and meme?
qa.a: Abhinav would see a claim repeated so often that it replaced his actual promise to freeze fees and turned him into the enemy without proof.

grounding: Shows a young adult who, after seeing one slogan repeated everywhere, votes against a candidate on a claim she never checked.

"Don't eat that," Maria said, pushing Jagdish's plate away. "The new contractor puts chemicals in everything. Everyone knows."
"Everyone who?"
"It's on every group. There were posters in the hostel. Sreeja said it, the seniors said it, it's literally everywhere."
"Okay. But what's the proof?"
Maria opened her mouth. Closed it. "It's just obvious. They're new, they're cutting costs."
"Did anyone test the food? Did anyone get sick?"
"I heard about some guy."
"Which guy?"
"I don't know his name." Maria frowned. "Wait. I've heard it so many times I stopped asking."
Jagdish shrugged. "I've eaten here every day for a month. And the old contractor's cousin runs the shop outside the gate. He printed those posters."
Maria stared at her samosa. "So I've been angry at these people for three weeks because of posters."
"Want to ask the student council to get the food checked? Then we'll actually know."

qa.q: Who printed the posters, according to Jagdish?
qa.a: The old contractor's cousin, who runs the shop outside the gate.

qa.q: What did Maria realise about her own certainty?
qa.a: Maria felt uneasy and a bit foolish, seeing that the claim had been heard so many times that asking for proof had stopped.

qa.q: What sensible step does Jagdish suggest?
qa.a: Asking the student council to get the food checked, so the claim is tested instead of just repeated.

qa.q: How might the new contractor be affected by the claim?
qa.a: The contractor could lose customers and be blamed without any proof, harmed by repetition alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult who came to accept a repeated claim about a clear villain as obvious, without any proof.
